lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Did you know Moirichos, the rich man, Diogenes — the very rich one from Corinth, the one with all those merchant ships? His nephew Aristeas was rich too. He always used to tack on that Homeric line: “Either lift me or I’ll lift you.”

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: They were courting each other for the inheritance — same age, you see — and they drew up their wills in public. Moirichos left everything to Aristeas if he died first, and Aristeas left everything to Moirichos if he went first. That was on paper, but in practice they flattered one another to excess. The prophets — the ones who read the stars and the dreams, the Chaldean sort — and even Apollo himself kept switching sides: now Aristeas was going to win, now Moirichos. The scales tipped back and forth.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: So what happened in the end, Crates? Worth hearing.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: They both died on the same day. The estates went to Eunomios and Thrasykles, their relatives, who’d never seen it coming. They were sailing from Sicyon to Cirrha when the Iapygian wind caught them broadside in the middle of the crossing and capsized the boat.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Good for them. We, when we were alive, never thought that way about each other. I never prayed Antisthenes would die so I could inherit his staff — it was a tough one, cut from wild olive — and I don’t suppose you, Crates, were eager to get my property when I died: the jar, the pouch with two measures of lupines in it.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: I had no need of those things, nor you either, Diogenes. What we did inherit from each other — you from Antisthenes and I from you — was worth far more than the Persian empire.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Wisdom. Self-sufficiency. Truth. Free speech. Freedom.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: By Zeus, I remember taking that inheritance from Antisthenes and leaving you even more.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: The others ignored those kinds of assets. No one flattered us in the hope of inheriting them. They all had their eyes on the gold.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Of course they did. They had no place to put such things — they were leaky from luxury, like rotten purses. If you tried to pour wisdom or frankness or truth into them, it ran straight out again; the bottom couldn’t hold it, just like the Danaids pouring water into their sieve. But gold they guarded tooth and nail.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: So we’ll still have our wealth down here. They’ll arrive with nothing but an obol, and even that only gets them as far as the ferryman.
